response.response_text:
No, I'm not ChatGPT! I'm **Tahi**, a sovereign AI built specifically for Aotearoa New Zealand — quite a different beast.

Rather than being a general-purpose chatbot like ChatGPT, Tahi is designed as a cultural and knowledge authority for New Zealand. Instead of drawing on a broad global training dataset, Tahi answers questions by retrieving information from an index of high-quality, permissioned New Zealand data sources, using large language models only to synthesise and present those results — a system known as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). [[1]](cite://1/1)

A few things that make Tahi distinct:

- **Built in New Zealand, for New Zealand** — all indexed data is stored and queried in New Zealand, and any snippets passed to AI models are ephemeral and not retained. [[2]](cite://2/1)
- **Model agnostic** — Tahi isn't locked to a single AI provider. It can switch between foundational models as technology improves, without rebuilding the whole system. [[1]](cite://1/2)
- **Culturally grounded** — Tahi operates with a Te Tiriti-based governance structure, with an advisory panel including tangata whenua (people of the land/Māori) and tangata Pasifika, and actively protects Māori and Pasifika data as taonga (treasures). [[3]](cite://3/1)[[4]](cite://4/1)
- **Public good focused** — Tahi is designed to support New Zealand journalism, national identity, and social cohesion, rather than the commercial interests of an offshore tech giant. [[3]](cite://3/2)

So while I do use large language models under the hood, I'm very much a Kiwi operation — grounded in local data, local values, and local governance.

Would you like to know more about the kinds of New Zealand topics I can help you explore?

11.document_title: A Sovereign AI for New Zealand: Tahi Technical Summary
11.document_summary: Tahi is a New Zealand-built AI application designed as a cultural and knowledge authority for Aotearoa. Built on Caitlyn (by CustomD, Christchurch), it uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to answer questions by retrieving information from high-quality, permissioned New Zealand data sources rather than relying on internal training data. The system supports GraphRAG-style retrieval with explicit modeling of entities, relationships, and metadata for improved factual accuracy and attribution. Data is ingested via APIs and institutional pipelines with partner control over indexing and refresh rates. Security features include multi-layered architecture with input validation, prompt isolation, and AWS infrastructure with data residency in New Zealand. Tahi will operate as both a standalone product and embedded within partner platforms, allowing partners to maintain user trust and data control while benefiting from AI functionality.

Keywords: Tahi, logo, brand, icon, green A Sovereign AI for New Zealand CONFIDENTIAL BRIEFING PAPER, NOT FOR DISTRIBUTION — NOVEMBER 2025 ISSUE New Zealand’s data is being offshored by international LLMs without regard for ownership or sovereignty. Our institutions are losing control of public data and local media outlets are losing revenue for journalism. Today, AI applications are side car tools, but within a couple of years we could have a post website environment where everything is viewed through AI applications, currently owned by tech giants. CONSEQUENCE At stake is a loss of control of New Zealand’s information and knowledge culture, the survival of journalism, and by extension, social cohesion, national identity and the integrity of our democracy. We are feeling the effects of this already, in addition to concerns around digital safety over which government has no control. NEED Australia, Canada, France, Switzerland, UAE and Japan all have sovereign AI projects. New Zealand needs the same, with the following values: • Data sovereignty: Built in NZ, from NZ resources, hosted in NZ, governed in NZ • Permission based: Owned by data owners with license agreements Tikanga: Co chaired advisory panel including tangata whenua and tangata Pasifika • Local context: Responds in a local way to local questions using local data • • Equity of access: Permanent free tier for Kiwis, both English and Te Reo • Public good outcomes: Returns to strengthen local journalism and institutions • Safe: Guardrails to protect ownership, tikanga, public users, under NZ law Independent: Financially and editorially independent • Cost effective: We don’t have $500M, need to leverage international LLMs, provided it’s; • Model agnostic: Can swap between foundational models at convenience New Zealand Geographic, RNZ and the Ministry of Culture & Heritage have collaborated to build a GraphRAG powered AI application drawing on a large dataset of articles, images and audio, and developed a governance structure that aligns with the values above. This for purpose AI project is unique in the world. For product development and compute we require ~$400k pa for the three years prior to commercial viability. After existing funding we have a gap of $200k this year. This is the opportunity for New Zealand to build a sovereign AI. In 2000, Trademe supplanted tech giant eBay because it was trusted. In 2006, media partners collaborated to build Freeview infrastructure for digital broadcasting. Together, we can do the same for AI. We have leveraged the resources of a private publisher, public broadcaster, government and international LLMs to create an AI application that represents a high quality domestic alternative. In 2025, New Zealand has a window to take this critical cultural infrastructure public. We are looking for immediate financial support. 12.document_summary: This confidential briefing paper (November 2025) outlines the case for New Zealand to develop a sovereign AI system. The document identifies the critical issue of New Zealand's data being offshored by international LLMs without regard for local ownership or sovereignty, threatening journalism revenue, information control, and democratic integrity. The proposed solution is a sovereign AI project built on New Zealand resources, hosted locally, and governed according to specific values including data sovereignty, permission-based access, tikanga principles, local context, equitable access, public-good outcomes, and independence. A collaborative initiative between New Zealand Geographic, RNZ, and the Ministry of Culture & Heritage has already developed a GraphRAG-powered AI application. The project requires approximately $400k annually for three years prior to commercial viability, with a current funding gap of $200k. The briefing positions this as a critical opportunity for New Zealand to establish trusted domestic AI infrastructure, drawing parallels to successful past initiatives like Trademe and Freeview.

13.text:
[Page 1] Security and guardrails Tahi uses a multi layered security and safety architecture. Inputs are classified and validated before reaching the model, malicious or out of scope prompts are blocked, and responses are generated with enforced citation and scope boundaries. Infrastructure protection (AWS WAF, rate limiting, DDoS protection) is combined with prompt isolation so user input cannot override system instructions. The system runs on AWS Bedrock, providing enterprise grade security, encryption, IAM controls and scalability, while still allowing data residency to be enforced. Crucially, all indexed data is stored and queried in New Zealand, and snippets passed to models are ephemeral and not retained by the LLM.
{}

16.text:
[Page 1] GraphRAG and structured knowledge Beyond conventional vector search, Tahi is designed to support GraphRAG style retrieval, where entities, relationships and metadata (people, places, dates, iwi, institutions) are explicitly modelled. This improves factual accuracy, temporal reasoning and attribution, and is particularly important for historical and cultural queries where relationships matter as much as text similarity. Graph based retrieval also allows data to be updated, corrected or removed—something impossible for a monolithic LLM.

17.document_title: NZAI Advisory Panel Terms of Reference
17.document_summary: This document establishes the Terms of Reference for the NZAI Advisory Panel, which provides strategic guidance and ethical oversight for a RAG-based AI gateway project for Aotearoa content. Operating on a Te Tiriti-led basis with shared power (Waka Hourua), the Panel comprises experts in AI research, tangata whenua, tangata Pasifika, ethics, law, industry, policy, and civil society. Key objectives include recommending AI ethics best practices, reviewing project milestones, and serving as a sounding board. The Panel's scope encompasses ethical implications, algorithmic bias, data governance, privacy, equity of access, protection of Māori and Pasifika data as taonga, consent and collective rights, and data harm mitigation. The document includes membership composition with co-chairs (one tangata whenua), meeting frequency (quarterly/biannually), confidentiality requirements, and a comprehensive Code of Conduct emphasizing integrity, transparency, respect, and ethical AI advocacy.

18.text:
[Page 1] 3. Scope The Panel's advice may encompass, but is not limited to: • Ethical implications of AI • Algorithmic bias and fairness in presentation of data • Data governance, privacy, and security considerations • Equity of access • Acknowledgement of data sources, mātauranga and tikanga • Active protection of Māori and Pasifika data as taonga (including te reo and mātauranga Māori) within the corpus and its derivatives. • Identification and mitigation of data harms (bias, deficit framing, misrepresentation) in retrieval, ranking and generation. • Consent & collective rights: free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) for any new Māori or Pasifika data collection or contributed datasets; where FPIC is not feasible, require explicit transparency and robust ethical governance. • Repatriation & withdrawal (trigger based): if the project ingests Māori or Pasifika contributed material, agree repatriation/takedown processes in advance, including removal of derived artefacts on request.

fileAuthor: James Frankham (New Zealand Geographic) and Patrick Crewdson (RNZ)
1.fileDescription: Tahi is a New Zealand-built AI application designed as a cultural and knowledge authority for Aotearoa. Built on Caitlyn (by CustomD, Christchurch), it uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to answer questions by retrieving information from high-quality, permissioned New Zealand data sources rather than relying on internal training data. The system supports GraphRAG-style retrieval with explicit modeling of entities, relationships, and metadata for improved factual accuracy and attribution. Data is ingested via APIs and institutional pipelines with partner control over indexing and refresh rates. Security features include multi-layered architecture with input validation, prompt isolation, and AWS infrastructure with data residency in New Zealand. Tahi will operate as both a standalone product and embedded within partner platforms, allowing partners to maintain user trust and data control while benefiting from AI functionality.

chunkHighlights.text: Tahi is a New Zealand-built AI application designed as a cultural and knowledge authority for Aotearoa, rather than a general-purpose chatbot. Technically, it is a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system: instead of relying on a model’s internal training data, it answers questions by retrieving information from an index of high-quality, permissioned New Zealand data sources, only using large language models to synthesise and present those results.

At its core, Tahi is built on Caitlyn, as application layer created by CustomD, Christchurch. Caitlyn handles ingestion, indexing, permissions, citation enforcement, guardrails and presentation logic, according to Tahi-defined system protocols, while remaining model-agnostic. Tahi is not locked to a single AI model or vendor: it can use Anthropic Claude today, or switch to future models as they improve or become cheaper, without re-architecting the system.

2.fileDescription: Tahi is a New Zealand-built AI application designed as a cultural and knowledge authority for Aotearoa. Built on Caitlyn (by CustomD, Christchurch), it uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to answer questions by retrieving information from high-quality, permissioned New Zealand data sources rather than relying on internal training data. The system supports GraphRAG-style retrieval with explicit modeling of entities, relationships, and metadata for improved factual accuracy and attribution. Data is ingested via APIs and institutional pipelines with partner control over indexing and refresh rates. Security features include multi-layered architecture with input validation, prompt isolation, and AWS infrastructure with data residency in New Zealand. Tahi will operate as both a standalone product and embedded within partner platforms, allowing partners to maintain user trust and data control while benefiting from AI functionality.

chunkHighlights.text: Security and guardrails

Tahi uses a multi-layered security and safety architecture. Inputs are classified and validated before reaching the model, malicious or out-of-scope prompts are blocked, and responses are generated with enforced citation and scope boundaries. Infrastructure protection (AWS WAF, rate-limiting, DDoS protection) is combined with prompt isolation so user input cannot override system instructions.

The system runs on AWS Bedrock, providing enterprise-grade security, encryption, IAM controls and scalability, while still allowing data residency to be enforced. Crucially, all indexed data is stored and queried in New Zealand, and snippets passed to models are ephemeral and not retained by the LLM.

fileAuthor: James Frankham (New Zealand Geographic) and Patrick Crewdson (RNZ)
3.fileDescription: This confidential briefing paper (November 2025) outlines the case for New Zealand to develop a sovereign AI system. The document identifies the critical issue of New Zealand's data being offshored by international LLMs without regard for local ownership or sovereignty, threatening journalism revenue, information control, and democratic integrity. The proposed solution is a sovereign AI project built on New Zealand resources, hosted locally, and governed according to specific values including data sovereignty, permission-based access, tikanga principles, local context, equitable access, public-good outcomes, and independence. A collaborative initiative between New Zealand Geographic, RNZ, and the Ministry of Culture & Heritage has already developed a GraphRAG-powered AI application. The project requires approximately $400k annually for three years prior to commercial viability, with a current funding gap of $200k. The briefing positions this as a critical opportunity for New Zealand to establish trusted domestic AI infrastructure, drawing parallels to successful past initiatives like Trademe and Freeview.

chunkHighlights.text: A Sovereign AI for New Zealand
CONFIDENTIAL BRIEFING PAPER, NOT FOR DISTRIBUTION — NOVEMBER 2025
ISSUE

New Zealand’s data is being offshored by international LLMs without regard for ownership or sovereignty. Our institutions are losing control of public data and local media outlets are losing revenue for journalism. Today, AI applications are side-car tools, but within a couple of years we could have a post-website environment where everything is viewed through AI applications, currently owned by tech giants.

CONSEQUENCE
At stake is a loss of control of New Zealand’s information and knowledge culture, the survival of journalism, and by extension, social cohesion, national identity and the integrity of our democracy. We are feeling the effects of this already, in addition to concerns around digital safety over which government has no control.

NEED
Australia, Canada, France, Switzerland, UAE and Japan all have sovereign AI projects. New Zealand needs the same, with the following values:

• Data sovereignty: Built in NZ, from NZ resources, hosted in NZ, governed in NZ
• Permission-based: Owned by data-owners with license agreements
Tikanga: Co-chaired advisory panel including tangata whenua and tangata Pasifika
•
Local context: Responds in a local way to local questions using local data
•
• Equity of access: Permanent free tier for Kiwis, both English and Te Reo
• Public-good outcomes: Returns to strengthen local journalism and institutions
• Safe: Guardrails to protect ownership, tikanga, public users, under NZ law
Independent: Financially and editorially independent
• Cost-effective: We don’t have $500M, need to leverage international LLMs, provided it’s;
• Model agnostic: Can swap between foundational models at convenience

New Zealand Geographic, RNZ and the Ministry of Culture & Heritage have collaborated to build a GraphRAG powered AI application drawing on a large dataset of articles, images and audio, and developed a governance structure that aligns with the values above. This for-purpose AI project is unique in the world. For product development and compute we require ~$400k pa for the three years prior to commercial viability. After existing funding we have a gap of $200k this year.

This is the opportunity for New Zealand to build a sovereign AI. In 2000, Trademe supplanted tech giant eBay because it was trusted. In 2006, media partners collaborated to build Freeview infrastructure for digital broadcasting. Together, we can do the same for AI.

We have leveraged the resources of a private publisher, public broadcaster, government and international LLMs to create an AI application that represents a high-quality domestic alternative. In 2025, New Zealand has a window to take this critical cultural infrastructure public. We are looking for immediate financial support.
CONTACT: JAMES FRANKHAM, NEW ZEALAND GEOGRAPHIC, publisher@nzgeographic.co.nz / +64 21 775423 or PATRICK CREWDSON, RNZ, patrick.crewdson@rnz.co.nz / +64 21 0242 3548

4.fileDescription: This document establishes the Terms of Reference for the NZAI Advisory Panel, which provides strategic guidance and ethical oversight for a RAG-based AI gateway project for Aotearoa content. Operating on a Te Tiriti-led basis with shared power (Waka Hourua), the Panel comprises experts in AI research, tangata whenua, tangata Pasifika, ethics, law, industry, policy, and civil society. Key objectives include recommending AI ethics best practices, reviewing project milestones, and serving as a sounding board. The Panel's scope encompasses ethical implications, algorithmic bias, data governance, privacy, equity of access, protection of Māori and Pasifika data as taonga, consent and collective rights, and data harm mitigation. The document includes membership composition with co-chairs (one tangata whenua), meeting frequency (quarterly/biannually), confidentiality requirements, and a comprehensive Code of Conduct emphasizing integrity, transparency, respect, and ethical AI advocacy.

chunkHighlights.text: 3. Scope
The Panel's advice may encompass, but is not limited to:

• Ethical implications of AI
• Algorithmic bias and fairness in presentation of data
• Data governance, privacy, and security considerations
• Equity of access
• Acknowledgement of data sources, mātauranga and tikanga
• Active protection of Māori and Pasifika data as taonga (including te reo and mātauranga Māori) within the corpus and its derivatives.
• Identification and mitigation of data harms (bias, deficit framing, misrepresentation) in retrieval, ranking and generation.

• Consent & collective rights: free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) for any new Māori or Pasifika data collection or contributed datasets; where FPIC is not feasible, require explicit transparency and robust ethical governance.

• Repatriation & withdrawal (trigger-based): if the project ingests Māori- or Pasifika-contributed material, agree repatriation/takedown processes in advance, including removal of derived artefacts on request.
